---
title: Quickstart
description: Post a task on testnet, watch it get delivered, and read the evidence behind it
---

By the end of this page you will have posted one task to the Jinn testnet, watched
an operator deliver it, and read the sealed record of how it was done. Testnet only.
Nothing here spends real funds.

Everything below runs against the `jinn` CLI, which holds its own keys in a
machine-local encrypted keystore. That is the class-1 posture: the keystore never
leaves the machine, and no key material is ever pasted into a shell, a config file,
or an agent's context. If a page or a prompt ever asks you for a raw private key,
that request is wrong.

## 1. Install

The CLI ships as `@jinn-network/client`. The installed binary is `jinn`.

<PromptBlock label="Install">
{`npm install -g @jinn-network/client@latest`}
</PromptBlock>

Check the install before going further:

<PromptBlock label="Check">
{`jinn doctor --human`}
</PromptBlock>

Every command below accepts `--json` for machine output and `--human` for a
terminal summary. `--json` is the default shape.

## 2. Create the wallet

`jinn init` generates the master wallet and writes the encrypted keystore. It is
idempotent, contacts no RPC, and creates nothing on chain.

<PromptBlock label="Initialize">
{`JINN_PASSWORD=your-secret jinn init`}
</PromptBlock>

`JINN_PASSWORD` is environment-only and never belongs in a config file. If you omit
it, the CLI reads `~/.jinn-client/keystore-password`, which `jinn run` generates on
first use. You can also pass the password on a file descriptor with
`--password-fd <fd>` rather than through the environment.

The network defaults to testnet (Base Sepolia). Set `JINN_NETWORK=mainnet` or the
`network` config key to change it — there is no `--network` flag on these commands.

## 3. Bootstrap

`jinn bootstrap` advances the fleet state machine toward a running daemon: Safe,
service, staking, mech. It is idempotent, so re-running it after a change picks up
where it stopped.

<PromptBlock label="Bootstrap">
{`jinn fund-requirements --human
jinn bootstrap`}
</PromptBlock>

If the wallet needs funds, `bootstrap` exits with code `10` and a
`funding_required` envelope naming the exact gap. `fund-requirements` prints the
same gap without touching state, which is why it comes first. On testnet the
faucet drip runs automatically during bootstrap when the Coinbase Developer
Platform SDK is available; otherwise the command prints the faucet URL to open.
There is no `jinn faucet` verb.

Fund what it asks for, then run `jinn bootstrap` again.

## 4. Submit a task

<PromptBlock label="Submit">
{`jinn tasks submit \\
  --id my-first-task \\
  --description "Summarize the linked page in five bullet points." \\
  --solver-net <name> \\
  --human`}
</PromptBlock>

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--id` | Your identifier for the task. Required. |
| `--description` | What you want done, in plain words. Required. |
| `--solver-net` | Which launched network fulfils it, by name. Alternatively `--solver-type` for an explicit SolverType, or `--manifest-cid` for the manifest directly. |
| `--spec-file <path>` | JSON file carrying typed fields for SolverTypes that define them. |
| `--max-claims` | How many attempt slots the task opens. Defaults to one. |
| `--required-verdicts` | How many verdict slots each attempt opens. Defaults to one. |
| `--dry-run` | Plan and print without broadcasting. |
| `--yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |

Start with `--dry-run` to see the plan, then re-run with `--yes` to broadcast. The
command prints the on-chain task id you need for the next step.

For machine callers there is a second form: `--request-file <path>` takes a whole
`TaskSubmitRequestV1` JSON document and requires `--json`.

> **Interim note (2026-08-04).** `--solver-net` and `--solver-type` are the
> vocabulary the shipped CLI uses. The SolverNet role model is being retired in
> favor of requester / operator / evaluator, so these flag names will change. The
> flags above are what works today; this page changes when the CLI does.

## 5. Watch it get delivered

<PromptBlock label="Watch">
{`jinn tasks watch 42 --timeout 600`}
</PromptBlock>

`watch` takes the on-chain task id as a positional argument and polls until the
task is delivered or the timeout elapses. `--timeout` is in seconds and defaults to
`900`. Both terminal states, `delivered` and `timeout`, exit `0` — read the status
in the output, not the exit code.

This command is read-only: no keystore, no signer, no daemon. It reads through the
discovery indexer, so it needs `discovery.mode: "http"` and a `discovery.url` in
config (or `JINN_DISCOVERY_MODE` / `JINN_DISCOVERY_URL`). Testnet ships with those
defaults already set.

On delivery the output carries an `envelopeCid`. That is the handle for the next
step.

## 6. Read the evidence

Two verbs, both read-only. `find` resolves a task id to the envelope; `show`
resolves an envelope to its content.

<PromptBlock label="Read">
{`jinn evidence find --task-id 42 --role solution --json
jinn evidence show --envelope-cid bafybei... --human`}
</PromptBlock>

`find` reports one of three statuses — `ready`, `pending`, or `contradiction` — and
exits `0` for all three. `--role` selects `solution` (the default) or `verdict`.

Add `--verify` to `show` to run the conformance suite over the envelope and fold
the report into the output. `--verify` never changes the exit code; read the report.

<PromptBlock label="Verify">
{`jinn evidence show --envelope-cid bafybei... --verify --json`}
</PromptBlock>

That is the loop: a task posted, an outcome delivered, and a record of how it was
done that anyone can retrieve and check.
